language_wrapper: An explorer must traverse a rectangular grid of {rows} rows and {cols} columns of unit squares. The explorer may begin each attempt at any chosen square in row 1, and may move one square at a time (up, down, left, or right), revisiting squares if desired. Among the middle rows 2 through {rows_minus_1}, exactly {bad_cols} distinct columns each contain a single invisible teleport gate (located at an arbitrary, adversarially chosen middle-row position within that column), while the remaining {safe_cols} columns contain no gate at all. No column contains more than one gate, but a row may contain gates in multiple columns. If the explorer ever steps on a gate, the explorer is immediately returned to the chosen start square and that attempt ends; the location of the touched gate is then perfectly recorded and remembered for all future attempts. Reaching any square in row {rows} ends the process successfully. The total number {bad_cols} of gated columns is known in advance to the explorer. In the worst case over all placements of the gates consistent with these rules, determine the minimal number k of attempts required by an optimal strategy to guarantee success. Output this minimal k.
teacher_generator_code:
def generator(rng):
    # Choose reasonably sized parameters ensuring at least one safe column and nontrivial difficulty
    while True:
        rows = rng.randint(5, 300)  # at least 5 rows, plenty of middle rows
        cols = rng.randint(4, 300)  # at least 4 columns
        # choose bad_cols between 2 and min(cols-1, 80) to avoid trivial cases and keep variety
        max_bad = cols - 1
        if max_bad < 2:
            continue
        upper = min(max_bad, 80)
        bad_cols = rng.randint(2, upper)
        safe_cols = cols - bad_cols
        if safe_cols >= 1 and rows >= 3:
            break
    return {
        'rows': rows,
        'cols': cols,
        'bad_cols': bad_cols,
        'rows_minus_1': rows - 1,
        'safe_cols': safe_cols
    }
hardness_rationale: The seed problem features exactly one gate per middle row and no two in the same column, leading to a nontrivial but constant worst-case answer (3) from subtle path-planning and detour considerations. This generalization inverts and strengthens the adversarial aspect: exactly a known number of columns contain one gate each (at arbitrary middle-row positions), while multiple gates can now occupy the same row. Proving the minimal worst-case attempts requires an adversarial lower bound argument that leverages the per-column constraint (constructing a worst-case configuration aligned to the algorithm’s chosen columns) and a matching upper-bound strategy that systematically exhausts all gated columns. The necessity to reason about information acquisition across attempts, set-identification of bad columns, and the impossibility of learning more than one gate per attempt under the immediate-teleport rule makes the family more challenging conceptually than the seed.
notes:
Proof of correctness for k = bad_cols + 1.

Upper bound (strategy): The explorer maintains a set S of columns known to contain gates. On each attempt t = 1,2,..., select any column not in S and march straight down from row 1 to row rows. If the chosen column is safe, the explorer reaches the last row and succeeds. If it is gated, the explorer is teleported at the unique gate within that column; its location is recorded, and the column is added to S. Because each column holds at most one gate, every failure reveals exactly one new gated column and never contradicts prior information. After exactly bad_cols such failures, S equals the set of all bad columns. On the next attempt, any column outside S is guaranteed safe, so a straight descent succeeds. Hence k <= bad_cols + 1.

Lower bound (adversarial): Consider any (possibly adaptive) strategy for choosing paths over attempts. For the i-th distinct column the strategy first uses (over all attempts), the adversary places that column’s unique gate at the earliest middle-row cell encountered by the path in that column. This placement is feasible because different columns are independent (at most one gate per column), and multiple columns may have gates in the same row (rows are unconstrained). Under this placement, each time the strategy first employs a yet-untested bad column, the attempt immediately fails at its earliest encounter, revealing only that column’s gate. Since exactly bad_cols columns are gated, the adversary can ensure that the first bad_cols distinct columns chosen by the strategy are all gated, forcing at least bad_cols failed attempts before any safe column is ever tried. Therefore k >= bad_cols + 1.

Combining the bounds gives the exact worst-case minimal number of attempts k = bad_cols + 1.

Generalization explanation: Relative to the seed, we remove the inter-row exclusivity (one gate per row) and enforce a stronger per-column constraint with a known total number of gated columns. This change makes the adversary’s lower bound construction sharper and the optimal strategy an instance of set identification under one-bit-per-attempt feedback, elevating the combinatorial reasoning compared to the original constant bound.
source_question: An explorer is challenging to pass through a maze composed of 3033 rows and 3032 columns of squares. The rules of the maze are as follows: In all the middle rows (that is, from the 2nd row to the 3032nd row), there is one invisible teleportation gate hidden in each row, and there are no multiple invisible teleportation gates in the same column. The explorer starts from any position in the 1st row. Each time, he can move one square up, down, left or right, and it is allowed to pass through the explored areas repeatedly. If the explorer touches a teleportation gate, he will immediately return to the starting point and start the next attempt. However, the explorer will mark the position of that teleportation gate. If the explorer reaches any position in the 3033rd row, he will directly pass the maze. It is known that the explorer can remember the positions of all the discovered teleportation gates. Please construct a general strategy so that no matter how the teleportation gates are distributed, the explorer will definitely pass the maze in the \(k\)th attempt in the worst-case scenario. Find the minimum possible value of \(k\).
